parole.significato: Forms nouns for a discrete living organism that has a specified mode of living.
parole.testo: Probably from German, modification of Ancient Greek βῐούντ- (bĭoúnt-), βιῶν (biôn, “living”), present participle of βῐοῦν (bĭoûn, “to live”), from βῐ́ος (bĭ́os, “mode of life”).

parole.significato: The theory that humanity's morality will never advance beyond its present state.
parole.testo: From German Abderitismus, from Abderit (“foolish person”) + -ismus (“-ism”), from Ancient Greek Ἀβδηρῑ́της (Abdērī́tēs, “Abderite”) because of the Abderites’ famed foolishness and stupidity in classical Greece. It is equivalent to Abderite + -ism. The German term was coined by the philosopher Immanu

parole.significato: Total color blindness; the total inability to distinguish colors due to the absence of cone cells in the eyes.
parole.testo: From German Achromatopsie, from Ancient Greek ἀχρώματος (akhrṓmatos), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”), + -opsie. By surface analysis, a- + chromato- + -opsia.

parole.significato: meticulous, painstaking, thorough
parole.testo: From German akribisch (“meticulous”) or its etymon Ancient Greek ἀκριβής (akribḗs, “exact, accurate, precise”).

parole.significato: A base, C₅H₅N₅, found in certain glands and tissues, which pairs with thymine in DNA and uracil in RNA.
parole.testo: From German Adenin, from Ancient Greek ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”). By surface analysis, aden- + -ine. It was named in 1885 by the German biochemist Albrecht Kossel, in reference to the pancreas (a specific gland) from which Kossel's sample had been extracted.

parole.significato: a cell that divides by schizogony
parole.testo: From German Agamont, analyzable as Ancient Greek ἄγαμος (ágamos, “unmarried”) + -ont.

parole.significato: Accentuating a note by extending it slightly beyond its normal time value.
parole.testo: Apparently from German Agoge (“tempo”), from Ancient Greek ἀγωγή (agōgḗ, “carrying, leading, reduplicated formation; tempo”), + -ic, after German agogisch. By surface analysis, agoge + -ic.

parole.significato: A retroflexion of the face at the front of the palate in primates.
parole.testo: Coined by Austrian zoologist Helmut Otto Hofer in 1952 as German Airorhynchie, from Ancient Greek ἀείρω (aeírō, “to raise, lift”) + ῥῠ́γχος (rhŭ́nkhos, “snout”).

parole.significato: abnormal bluish pigmentation in fish, caused by lack of guanine
parole.testo: From German Alampie, coined (as Alampia) by Karl Theodor Ernst von Siebold (1863), from Ancient Greek α- (a-, “not”) + λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”).

parole.significato: A protective substance that exists in the serum or other bodily fluid and is capable of killing microorganisms; complem…
parole.testo: Ultimately from German Alexine, coined by Hans Buchner in 1891 from the Ancient Greek ἀλέξω (aléxō).

parole.significato: A physical condition that causes a person to gain sexual pleasure by suffering pain, particularly to erogenous zones.
parole.testo: From German Algolagnie, from Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”) + λαγνεία (lagneía, “lust”). Equivalent to algo- + -lagnia.

parole.significato: homogentisic acid
parole.testo: From German Alkapton, coined by Boedeker (1861) as "an admittedly somewhat barbaric combination" of Alkali (“alkali”) + Ancient Greek κάπτον (kápton), neuter present participle of Ancient Greek κάπτω (káptō, “to gulp down”), after the tendency of alkapton to strongly react with oxygen in alkaline so

parole.significato: A calcium fluoride phosphate of variable composition, sometimes used in the manufacture of fertilizer, as a gemstone, a…
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, from German Apatit (“apatite”). Apatit was coined by the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner (1749–1817), as follows: Ancient Greek ᾰ̓πᾰ́τη (ăpắtē, “deceit, fraud”) (as it is often mistaken for other minerals) + German -it (suffix forming nouns denoting

parole.significato: The perception of or belief in connectedness among unrelated phenomena.
parole.testo: From German Apophänie, from Ancient Greek ἀποφαίνω (apophaínō, “to appear”), from ἀπο- (apo-) and φαίνω (phaínō, “appear”), coined by German psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958.

parole.significato: A European, especially German, pharmacy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Apotheke. Doublet of bodega and boutique.

parole.significato: An amino acid found in animal foods that plays an important role in several physiological processes.
parole.testo: From German Arginin, from Ancient Greek ἄργυρος (árguros, “silver”) and ἀργινόεις (arginóeis, “silvery, brightly shining”) in reference to arginine nitrate crystals' silver-white appearance when first refined from lupin seedlings by Ernst Schulze and Ernst Steiger in 1886.

parole.significato: Possessing the property it describes.
parole.testo: From German autologisch, from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós, “self”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”), by surface analysis, autology + -ical.

parole.significato: A sulfur-containing member of the vitamin B complex, 5-[(3aS,4S,6aR)-2-oxohexahydro-1H-thieno[3,4-d]imidazol-4-yl]penta…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Biotin, from Ancient Greek βίοτος (bíotos, “life”) + the suffix -in.

parole.significato: An abrupt loss of muscle tone, sometimes associated with narcolepsy.
parole.testo: From German Kataplexie, from Ancient Greek κατάπληξις (katáplēxis), from κατά (katá, “down”) + πλῆξῐς (plêxĭs, “blow, act of striking”).

parole.significato: Any of a family of proteases primarily active within lysosomes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Kathepsin, from Ancient Greek καθέψω (kathépsō), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕψω (hépsō, “boil”).

parole.significato: The central region of a eukaryotic chromosome where the kinetochore is assembled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Centromer, corresponding to centro- + -mere (from Ancient Greek μέρος (méros, “part”)).

parole.significato: A complex of DNA, RNA and proteins within the cell nucleus out of which chromosomes condense during cell division.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Chromatin, from (combining form of) Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”) + -ινος (-inos, “made of”). Analyzable as chromatic (“of colour”) + -in (“substance”).

parole.significato: A linear arrangement of condensed DNA and associated proteins (such as chaperone proteins) which contains the genetic m…
parole.testo: 19th century: from German Chromosom, ultimately from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”) + σῶμα (sôma, “body”) (because they are stained under the microscope). Equivalent to chromo- + -some.

parole.significato: Having fleshy / succulent stems
parole.testo: From German chylocaul (from chyl- + Ancient Greek καυλός (kaulós, “stem”)) + English -ous.

parole.significato: A pale yellow oily liquid, containing phenols and similar compounds, obtained by the destructive distillation of wood t…
parole.testo: From German Kreosot in the 1830s, coined in 1832 by German natural philosopher Carl Ludwig, Baron Reichenbach, from Ancient Greek κρέας (kréas, “flesh”) + σωτήρ (sōtḗr, “preserver”) for its use as an antiseptic and meat-preservative. The creosote bush was named after its scent. By surface analysis,

parole.significato: A heterocyclic base, 4-aminopyrimidin-2(1H)-one, which pairs with guanine in DNA and RNA (by means of three hydrogen bo…
parole.testo: After German Cytosin, equivalent to Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos) + -ine. Cytosine was discovered and named by the German biochemists Albrecht Kossel and Albert Neumann in 1894 when it was hydrolyzed from calf thymus tissues.

parole.significato: That stimulates each ear with a different pitch or loudness
parole.testo: From German dichotisch, from Ancient Greek δῐ́χᾰ (dĭ́khă, “apart”) + οὖς (oûs), ὠτ- (ōt-, “ear”) + -isch (-ic).

parole.significato: The branch of biology dealing with the relationships of organisms with their environment and with each other.
parole.testo: Calque of German Ökologie (coined in 1866 by Ernst Haeckel), from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”). By surface analysis, eco- + -logy.

parole.significato: Marked by or resulting from extraordinary ability to recall detailed and vivid mental images of visual images.
parole.testo: From German eidetisch, from Ancient Greek εἰδητικός (eidētikós), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”).

parole.significato: A nucleus and the cytoplasm with which it interacts, considered as a unit.
parole.testo: From German Energid, from Ancient Greek ἐνεργός (energós, “active”) + German -id (= English -id).

parole.significato: A postulated physical or biochemical change in neural tissue that represents a memory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Engramm which was coined by German evolutionary biologist Richard Semon in 1904. First attested in English in 1921 (see quotation below). Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + γράμμα (grámma, “writing, picture”).

parole.significato: A measure of the disorder present in a system.
parole.testo: First attested in 1867, as the translation of German Entropie, coined in 1865 by Rudolph Clausius in analogy to Energie (“energy”), replacing the root of Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon, “work”) by Ancient Greek τροπή (tropḗ, “transformation”)).

parole.significato: A biomolecule that catalyses a biological chemical reaction: either a globular protein with this function or an RNA mol…
parole.testo: From German Enzym, coined 1878 by the German physiologist Wilhelm Kühne from Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + ζύμη (zúmē, “leaven”). By surface analysis, en- + zyme.

parole.significato: A red, acidic dye commonly used in histological stains.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Eosin, coined by Heinrich Caro, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + -in.

parole.significato: A worldwide change in sea level, especially one caused by melting ice or tectonic activity.
parole.testo: A back-formation from eustatic (borrowed from German eustatische (“eustatic”), from Ancient Greek εὖ (eû, “well, good”) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”)) + -y.

parole.significato: A stage in the development of embryos of most animals consisting of a three-layered sac of ectoderm, mesoderm and endod…
parole.testo: From German Gastrula, coined by Ernst Haeckel in his 1872 work "Biology of Calcareous Sponges". From gastr- (from Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr, “stomach”) + Latin -ula.

parole.significato: Humic acid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Geïn, coined by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1832, from Ancient Greek γήινος (gḗinos, “of earth”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”).

parole.significato: A theoretical unit of heredity of living organisms which may take several values and (in principle) predetermines a pre…
parole.testo: From German Gen, from Ancient Greek γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”), from the aorist infinitive of γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to come into being”). Coined by Danish botanist Wilhelm Ludwig Johannsen in 1909, in a German-language publication, from the last syllable of pangene.

parole.significato: A greenish form of mica found in greensand.
parole.testo: From German Glaukonit, from Ancient Greek γλαυκός (glaukós, “blue-green”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Any small molecule that can elicit an immune response only when attached to a large carrier such as a protein.
parole.testo: Early 20th century: from German Hapten, from Ancient Greek ἅπτειν (háptein, “to fasten”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the period of the Greek culture, history, or art from after the death of Alexander the Great (323 B…
parole.testo: From German hellenistisch, from Ancient Greek Ἑλληνιστής (Hellēnistḗs, “one who uses the Greek language”), from Ἑλλάς (Hellás, “Greece”). By surface analysis, Hellenist + -ic.

parole.significato: Belief in or worship of one deity without denying the existence of other deities.
parole.testo: From German Henotheismus, coined in the 19th century by German philosopher Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling (1775–1854) from Ancient Greek ἕν (hén, stem of εἷς (heîs, “one”)) + German Theismus (“theism”, ultimately from Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”))).

parole.significato: The study of religious festivals.
parole.testo: From German Heortologie, from Ancient Greek ἑορτή (heortḗ, “festival”) + -ology.

parole.significato: A powerful and addictive drug derived from opium producing intense euphoria, classed as an illegal narcotic in most of…
parole.testo: Since the 1890s, by genericization from German Heroin, originally a trademark, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs, “hero”) and the suffix -in (“-ine”). Said to have been called thus to evoke quick and sweeping effect as a painkiller and cough suppressant (its original uses). Alternatively explained as a

parole.significato: Inflammation of the sweat glands.
parole.testo: First attested in 1894. From the German Hidradenitis (1865; also the etymologically more consistent Hidrotadenitis, 1893), ultimately representing the Ancient Greek roots ἱδρώς (hidrṓs, “sweat”, stem: ἱδρῶτ-, hidrōt-) + ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”, stem: ἀδεν-, aden-) + -ῖτις (-îtis, “[inflammatory] disease

parole.significato: Any of various simple water-soluble proteins that are rich in the basic amino acids lysine and arginine and are complex…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Histon, perhaps from Ancient Greek ἵστημι (hístēmi, “make stand”) or ἱστός (histós, “loom”).

parole.significato: An isoline joining points on a map with the same total transport costs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Isodapane, coined by Alfred Weber. Equivalent to iso- + Ancient Greek δαπάνη (dapánē, “cost”).

parole.significato: An isoline that joins points on a map where the individuals of a particular migratory species arrive at the same time e…
parole.testo: Refashioning of the earlier spelling isepiptesis, from German Isepiptesen used by Alexander von Middendorff in his 1855 work Die Isepiptesen Russlands, from iso- + Ancient Greek ἐπίπτησις (epíptēsis, “flying down upon”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + πτῆσῐς (ptêsĭs, “flight”), from πέτομαι (pétomai, “f

parole.significato: An isoline joining points on a map with the same transport costs for a particular product.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Isotim, coined by Alfred Weber. Equivalent to iso- + Ancient Greek τιμή (timḗ, “value”).

parole.significato: A monoclinic-prismatic mineral containing aluminum, calcium, hydrogen, iron, magnesium, manganese, oxygen, potassium, s…
parole.testo: From German Katoforite, that from Ancient Greek κατώφορος (katṓphoros, “having a downward tendency”), from κάτω (kátō, “downward”) and φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”), referring to the mineral's volcanic origin. The suffix -ite was already used for other minerals.

parole.significato: The protein of which hair and nails are composed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Keratin, from Ancient Greek κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + -in. Doublet of carat.

parole.significato: Any of a class of types of cancer affecting the blood cells, especially the white blood cells (usually with massive leu…
parole.testo: From German Leukämie, from Ancient Greek λευκός (leukós, “white”) + αἷμα (haîma, “blood”). By surface analysis, leuk- + -emia.

parole.significato: A petroleum fraction boiling 75°-125°C used as a solvent and fuel.
parole.testo: Attested since 1872, borrowed from German Ligroin, a trade mark of illuminating liquid hydrocarbon first attested in 1866 as Lygroin and Ligroine. Further origin uncertain, but possibly from Ancient Greek λιγυρός (ligurós, “clear”).

parole.significato: describing a liquid crystal that exhibits phase transitions as a function of concentration
parole.testo: From lyo- + -tropic, c. 1910, presumably borrowed from German, or by analogy with earlier lyo- terms such as lyophilic or lyophilization (1894). From Ancient Greek λύω (lúō, “to loosen, to dissolve”) + τροπικός (tropikós, “of or pertaining to a turn or change; or the solstice; or a trope or figure;

parole.significato: mast cell
parole.testo: From German Mastzelle f, "feeding cell," coined in 1878 by immunologist Paul Ehrlich; "Mast" + Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos, “cell”). Not a cognate with the Ancient Greek root μαστός (mastós, “(human) breast”).

parole.significato: The plant tissue composed of totipotent cells that allows plant growth.
parole.testo: From German Meristem, from Ancient Greek μεριστός (meristós, “divided”), from μερίζω (merízō), from μέρος (méros) + στέμμα (stémma, “wreath, garland”). First used in 1858 by Swiss botanist Carl Wilhelm von Nägeli (1817–1891).

parole.significato: A spherical or ovoid organelle found in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells and containing genetic material separate from…
parole.testo: From German Mitochondrium, coined by Carl Benda in 1898, from Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread”) + χονδρίον (khondríon), diminutive of χόνδρος (khóndros, “grain, morsel”).

parole.significato: The division of a cell nucleus in which the genome is copied and separated into two identical halves. It is normally fo…
parole.testo: From German Mitose, from Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread”) + -osis, probably in reference to the thread-like chromatin seen during mitosis.

parole.significato: The attainment of sexual pleasure from watching other people have sex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Mixoscopie, from Ancient Greek μίξις (míxis, “intercourse”) + German -skopie (“-scopy”). Reportedly coined by Albert Moll (1862–1939).

parole.significato: Persisting effect of memory of past events.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Mneme which was coined by German evolutionary biologist Richard Semon in 1904 from Ancient Greek μνήμη (mnḗmē). First attested in English in 1921 where it was capitalized Mneme.

parole.significato: any of a range of reddish-brown minerals that are mixed phosphates of the lighter rare earth elements lanthanum, cerium…
parole.testo: From German Monazit, from Ancient Greek μονάζω (monázō, “be solitary”).

parole.significato: The Orient; the East.
parole.testo: From morning + land, translating German Morgenland, Luther's translation of Ancient Greek ἀνατολή (anatolḗ, “(sun-)rising”).

parole.significato: Relating to the response of a plant to a stimulus that does not depend on the location of the stimulus.
parole.testo: From German nastisch from epinastisch, coined c.1854 by German botanist Karl Friedrich Schimper, from Ancient Greek ναστός (nastós, “pressed together”), from νάσσω (nássō, “to press, cram full”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Homo neanderthalensis.
parole.testo: From obsolete German Neanderthal, now spelled Neandertal, the name of a valley (German Tal, older also spelled Thal) near Düsseldorf where the first Neanderthal was discovered in 1856. A hollow near the valley was known as Neanderhöhle (“Neander Hollow”) and Neandershöhle (“Neander’s Hollow”) in the

parole.significato: The retention of juvenile characteristics in the adult.
parole.testo: From German Neotenie, coined in 1884 by anatomist Julius Kollmann from Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “young”) + τείνειν (teínein, “to extend, spread or tense”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a marine environment of shallow waters.
parole.testo: First attested in 1891. Borrowed from German neritisch, from Ancient Greek Νηρίτης (Nērítēs, “minor sea god”) + German -isch (“-ic”).

parole.significato: A thing as it is independent of any conceptualization or perception by the human mind, postulated by practical reason b…
parole.testo: From German Noumenon, from Ancient Greek νοούμενον (nooúmenon, “thing that is known”), passive present participle of νοέω (noéō, “I know”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the od or odyle (“a hypothetical force or natural power, now proved not to exist, which was suppose…
parole.testo: From odyle, odyl + -ic (suffix meaning of or pertaining to forming adjectives from nouns). Odyle, odyl is derived from od (borrowed from German Od, arbitrarily coined by the German scientist and philosopher Carl Reichenbach (1788–1869)) + Ancient Greek ῡ̔́λη (hū́lē, “wood; material, matter, substanc

parole.significato: A bird.
parole.testo: From German Ornis, from Ancient Greek ὄρνις (órnis, “bird”), Ancient Greek ὄρνιθος (órnithos, “bird”).

parole.significato: An allotrope of oxygen (symbol O₃) having three atoms in the molecule instead of the usual two; it is a toxic gas, gene…
parole.testo: From German Ozon, coined 1840 by Christian Friedrich Schönbein, from Ancient Greek ὄζον (ózon), neuter participle of ὄζω (ózō, “I smell”), in reference to its pungent odour. The “fresh air” sense is from an erroneous former belief that seaweed contains and releases ozone.

parole.significato: A belief in a god who is both pantheistic and deistic, in particular a god who designed the universe and then became it…
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from German Pandeismus, from pan- (from Ancient Greek παν- (pan-, prefix meaning ‘all’)) + Deismus (“deism”) (from Latin deus (“deity, god”) + German -ismus (“-ism”)). (Similar words appear earlier in various languages, but apparently not in the same sense.) The word can be analyse

parole.significato: A doctrine that the universe subsists within God, but that God nevertheless transcends or has some existence separate f…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Panentheismus, coined by Karl Christian Friedrich Krause in 1828 from Ancient Greek πᾶν ἐν θεῷ (pân en theōî, “all in god”) + -ismus (“-ism”).

parole.significato: The tendency to interpret a vague stimulus as something known to the observer, such as interpreting marks on Mars as ca…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Pareidolie, constructed from Ancient Greek παρα- (para-, “alongside”) + εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image”) + -ία (-ía). By surface analysis, par- + eidolia.

parole.significato: A digestive enzyme that chemically digests, or breaks down, proteins into shorter chains of amino acids.
parole.testo: From German Pepsin, corresponding to Ancient Greek πέψις (pépsis, “digestion”) + -in.

parole.significato: Any water-soluble mixture of polypeptides and amino acids formed by the partial hydrolysis of protein.
parole.testo: From German Pepton, from Ancient Greek πεπτόν (peptón, “cooked, digested”) derived from πέπτω (péptō, “soften, ripen, boil, cook, bake, digest”).

parole.significato: A vascular tissue in land plants primarily responsible for the distribution of sugars and nutrients manufactured in the…
parole.testo: First attested in 1872. From German Phloëm, coined by Swiss botanist Carl Nägeli in 1858 from Ancient Greek φλόος (phlóos, “husk, bark”) + a Greek-sounding ending -em (cf. System).

parole.significato: A mica mineral with the chemical formula KMg₃AlSi₃O₁₀(F,OH)₂, a basic potassium magnesium aluminosilicate, used as an i…
parole.testo: From German Phlogopit, from Ancient Greek φλογωπός (phlogōpós, “fiery-looking”) + -ite.

parole.significato: The evolutionary history of groups of organisms, such as species or clades.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Phylogenie, coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866, a neologism created as if borrowed from a Classic Greek word φυλογένεια (phulogéneia), composed from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “tribe, genus, species”) + -γένεια (-géneia, “-geny (generation, production)”), equivalent to phylo- + -

parole.significato: Organisms, especially small and microscopic ones, that drift in water.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Plankton, coined by German zoologist and marine biologist Victor Hensen. By surface analysis, Ancient Greek πλαγκτός (planktós, “drifter”) + -on. Ultimately from Ancient Greek πλαγκτόν (planktón, “drifting”), neuter nominative of πλαγκτός (planktós), from πλάζομαι (plázomai, “to

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to plankton.
parole.testo: From plankton + -ic, after German planktonisch. From Ancient Greek πλαγκτόν (planktón, “drifting”), neuter nominative of πλαγκτός (planktós), from πλάζομαι (plázomai, “to wander, drift”), from πλάζω (plázō, “to cause to wander, drive astray”).

parole.significato: Any of various organelles found in the cells of plants and algae, often used for photosynthesis.
parole.testo: From German Plastid, from Ancient Greek πλαστός (plastós), verbal adjective of πλάσσω (plássō).

parole.significato: The central portion of the apical meristem in a growing plant root or stem which, according to the histogen theory, giv…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Plerom + English -ome (suffix denoting a mass of something). Plerom is derived from Pleroma (obsolete), from Ancient Greek πλήρωμᾰ (plḗrōmă, “that which fills, a complement; a filling up, a completing”): see further at pleroma.

parole.significato: Acute infection by the poliovirus, especially of the motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem, leading to muscle…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Poliomyelitis, from the Ancient Greek πολιός (poliós, “grey”) + μυελός (muelós, “marrow”) + -ῖτις (-îtis, “-itis”). Compare French poliomyélite.

parole.significato: A geometric shape (of any number of dimensions) which is fully enclosed and has flat sides, making it a member of the g…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from German Polytop, originally coined by German mathematician Reinhold Hoppe in 1882, and first used in English by British mathematician Alicia Boole Stott in her 1910 paper Geometrical deduction of semiregular from regular polytopes and space fillings. By surface analysis, poly-

parole.significato: A government by, or dominated by, prostitutes or corrupt persons.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from German Pornokratie, first found in the writings of Austrian-born Biblical scholar Alfred Edersheim (1825–1889), from Ancient Greek πόρνη (pórnē, “female prostitute”) + -κρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (-krătĭ́ā, “-cracy”, suffix indicating “government, rule”); analysable as porno- + -cracy.

parole.significato: The entire contents of a cell comprising the nucleus and the cytoplasm. It is a semi-fluid, transparent substance which…
parole.testo: From German Protoplasma, coined by Czech physiologist Jan Evangelista Purkyně, from Ancient Greek πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) + πλάσμα (plásma, “something molded”). By surface analysis, proto- + -plasm. Compare also protoplasma, used in Late Latin for the “first-created one” (i.e. Adam).

parole.significato: Any plant which thrives in sandy conditions.
parole.testo: From German Psammophyt, containing Ancient Greek ψάμμος (psámmos, “sand”). By surface analysis, psammo- + -phyte.

parole.significato: A person with a personality disorder indicated by a pattern of lying, cunning, manipulating, glibness, exploiting, heed…
parole.testo: From German psychopathisch, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).

parole.significato: Any of a class of aromatic heterocyclic compounds containing a ring of four carbon atoms and a nitrogen atom; especiall…
parole.testo: From German Pyrrol, corresponding to Ancient Greek πυρρός (purrhós, “reddish, fiery”) + -ole.

parole.significato: An igneous, volcanic (extrusive) rock, of felsic composition, with aphanitic to porphyritic texture.
parole.testo: Coined by Ferdinand von Richthofen as German Rhyolith, from Ancient Greek ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”) + λίθος (líthos, “stone”) (modified to + -lite).

parole.significato: An aquatic sludge-like sediment rich in organic matter formed in oxygen-free areas at the bottom of lakes, seas etc.
parole.testo: From German Sapropel, corresponding to sapro- + Ancient Greek πηλός (pēlós, “mud, clay”).

parole.significato: Characterized by social withdrawal and emotional coldness or flattened affectivity.
parole.testo: From schiz(ophrenia)- + -oid, from German, from Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”) and εἶδος (eîdos, “form, likeness”).

parole.significato: A cell that divides by schizogony.
parole.testo: From German Schizont, from the present participle of Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “divide”). By surface analysis, schiz- + -ont.

parole.significato: A psychiatric diagnosis denoting a persistent, often chronic, mental illness characterised by abnormal perception, thin…
parole.testo: From German Schizophrenie (coined by Eugen Bleuler), from Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”) + φρήν (phrḗn, “mind, heart, diaphragm”) + English -ia. A combination of schizo- + -phrenia.

parole.significato: (containing) selenium
parole.testo: From German Selen (“selenium”); as above, also ultimately from Ancient Greek σελήνη (selḗnē, “moon”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a subdivision of Afroasiatic Semitic languages: Akkadian, Amharic, Arabic, Aramaic, Hebrew, Maltese…
parole.testo: From Semite + -ic (18th century), from German semitisch, from Ancient Greek Σήμ (Sḗm), from the Hebrew שֵׁם (Šēm, “Shem”), the name of the eldest son of Noah in biblical tradition (Genesis 5.32, 6.10, 10.21), considered the forefather of the Semitic peoples. parole.testo: Initially in cytology from German Syndesis, coined by Valentin Häcker in 1904 from Ancient Greek σύνδεσις (súndesis, “binding, joining”), from συνδεῖν (sundeîn, “to join, to bind”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, “-sis: forming nouns”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together”) + δεῖν (deîn, “to bind, to tie”). parole.significato: Reluctance or refusal to ascribe purpose to natural phenomena.
parole.testo: From German Teleophobie in the late 19th century. The OED considers the word modern Latin, but the earliest appearance is in the writing of Karl Ernst von Baer in German in the 1860s. parole.significato: A mixture of a metal and a metal oxide capable of producing a thermite reaction, such as aluminium metal and ferric oxi…
parole.testo: From German Thermit, from Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “heat”) + -it; comparable to English therm- + -ite.

parole.significato: Of or from the geologic strata above the Permian and below the Jurassic; of or belonging to the period 250 to 200 milli…
parole.testo: From Trias (“three-layered geologic strata between the Permian and Jurassic”) < German Trias < Ancient Greek τριάς (triás, “triad”), + -ic. Coined in 1841 by geologist Friedrich August von Alberti (1795–1878).

parole.significato: An animal that normally lives entirely in the dark parts of caves, often with no functioning eyes or no pigmentation.
parole.testo: From German Troglobie (from Ancient Greek τρώγλη (trṓglē, “hole”) + βίος (bíos, “life”)). By surface analysis, troglo- + -obe + -ite.

parole.significato: An essential amino acid with an indole side chain; present in many foods, especially chocolate, oats, banana and milk;…
parole.testo: From German Tryptophan, from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō, “to appear”).

parole.significato: Homosexuality.
parole.testo: From German Uranismus, from Ancient Greek οὐράνιος (ouránios, “heavenly, spiritual”).

parole.significato: A pre-reflective, original belief; a foundational doxic attitude prior to doubt or affirmation.
parole.testo: German Urdoxa, equivalent to ur- + doxa (Ancient Greek δόξα (dóxa)), in Husserlian phenomenology.

parole.significato: A vascular tissue in land plants primarily responsible for the distribution of water and minerals taken up by the roots…
parole.testo: From German Xylem, from Ancient Greek ξύλον (xúlon, “wood”).
